screens.title: Advanced OpenStack Operations, Monitoring, and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to operate and recover a production Red Hat OpenStack Platform cloud. We start by treating monitoring as the platform's sensory system: metrics and dashboards give you early warnings; centralized logs let you trace events across services; and a disciplined troubleshooting approach converts noisy alerts into root causes. You will see concrete examples with commands for identifying a Nova A P I failure, reading relevant service logs, and verifying dependent services like RabbitMQ and the database. We also cover backup components you must protect — databases, configuration files, and Glance images — and why Ceph's durability does not replace tested recovery procedures. Finally, you will learn upgrade and maintenance practices to reduce downtime and preserve a rollback path. As you follow the demonstrations, think about how your organization currently captures metrics, centralizes logs, and verifies recovery procedures. That question will guide the lab at the end: how would you adapt your backup strategy for OpenStack?

Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Overview
Advanced OpenStack Operations, Monitoring, and Troubleshooting
Operational practices to keep Red Hat OpenStack Platform resilient, observable, and recoverable.
In this lesson

You will master monitoring stacks, centralized logging, and a stepwise troubleshooting workflow. We will simulate a Nova API failure and walk through commands and configuration checks. Then we review backups, Ceph considerations, and upgrade practices.

Why it matters

Availability and fast recovery reduce customer impact and mean fewer fire drills. Observability and backups let you diagnose issues and restore service with confidence.

Quick Start

Begin by ensuring Prometheus scrapes service exporters and logs are centralized. Then verify database and message queue health before troubleshooting service failures.

Using CLI tools means you can run the openstack service list and inspect server, port, and agent status. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone you can use as a checklist during audits and drills. These skills reduce mean time to resolution, help you validate change plans, and make recovery predictable.

screens.title: Monitoring: the eyes and ears of RHOSP
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring is more than checking whether services are up. For a Red Hat OpenStack Platform cloud you must monitor service health, performance metrics like C P U, R A M, disk input and output and network throughput, and A P I response times. These signals let you detect slowdowns before they become outages. A common mistake is only collecting host-level metrics and neglecting service-specific metrics, such as Nova scheduler queue depth or Neutron agent heartbeats. To be effective, configure exporters that expose service metrics to Prometheus and create Grafana panels for latency, error rates, and message queue depth. Use service-specific alerts that combine conditions — for example, high A P I latency together with a RabbitMQ backlog — to reduce false positives. Concrete example: if Grafana shows rising Nova A P I latency and Prometheus shows a growing RabbitMQ queue, suspect a messaging bottleneck rather than a compute node fault. Misconception: monitoring is not a replacement for logging; logs give the causal trace you need for root cause. Key takeaway: instrument services and hosts, tune alerts to reduce noise, and correlate metrics with logs to find the true issue.

keyIdea.title: Monitor beyond 'up'
keyIdea.text: Track service-specific metrics and correlate them with host metrics to detect and diagnose emerging problems.

content.html:
Core Concept › Monitoring
Definition
Monitoring collects metrics and alerts on service and host behavior so operators can detect anomalies early and prioritize investigation.
  • • Monitor CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network throughput for hosts.
  • • Monitor service-specific metrics like API latency, queue depths, and agent heartbeats.
  • • Correlate metrics with logs to reach a root cause quickly.
Concrete Example

If Grafana shows increasing Nova API latency while Prometheus reports growing RabbitMQ queue length, prioritize investigating the message queue before rebooting compute services.

Prometheus + Grafana Pattern
Prometheus
Scrapes exporters, stores time-series metrics, supports alerts based on expressions.
Grafana
Visualizes metrics and builds panels that combine multiple metrics for context.
Alerting insight
Use compound alerts that require multiple signals, such as high API latency AND high queue depth, to reduce noisy pages.
Key Takeaway
Instrument services and hosts, then correlate metrics with logs to reduce investigation time.
Common Mistake
Relying only on host metrics and ignoring service-level signals leads to misdirected troubleshooting.
Pro Tip
Start with a small set of high-value dashboards: API latency, scheduler queue, agent heartbeats, and RabbitMQ depth.

screens.title: Prometheus and Grafana for RHOSP
screens.narratorSegment: Prometheus and Grafana form a compact monitoring architecture commonly used with Red Hat OpenStack Platform. Prometheus scrapes metrics from exporters exposed by OpenStack services or host exporters on RHEL. Those metrics are stored as time-series data and evaluated by alert rules. Grafana queries Prometheus to build dashboards that combine metrics across services. For example, a dashboard showing Nova A P I request latency, Nova scheduler backlog, and RabbitMQ queue depth gives a combined view that helps discriminate between compute, scheduling, and messaging problems. A common misstep is scraping only default exporters; ensure that service-specific exporters are enabled and that the scrape interval matches your alerting needs. Another practical tip: tag metrics with service and host labels so panels can filter by controller, compute, or storage nodes. Concrete example: set an alert for when Nova A P I p99 latency rises above a threshold while RabbitMQ queue length exceeds a limit; this pairing will point you to messaging saturation rather than transient compute slowness. Remember to archive long-term metrics if you need historical trend analysis during post-mortem investigations. Prometheus and Grafana for RHOSP means prometheus collects labeled metrics; grafana visualizes them. use combined panels and labels to find cause quickly.. In practical terms, how prometheus scrapes metrics and grafana surfaces service health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Prometheus collects labeled metrics; Grafana visualizes them. Use combined panels and labels to find cause quickly.

content.html:
Process Flow › Prometheus & Grafana
Architecture Summary

Prometheus scrapes exporters, stores time-series metrics, and triggers alerts. Grafana queries Prometheus and builds dashboards for context and trend analysis.

  • • Use exporters for Nova, Neutron, Cinder, Keystone, and host metrics.
  • • Label metrics with instance, host, and service roles.
  • • Archive long-term metrics for capacity planning.
Example Alert

Trigger when Nova API p99 latency is high AND RabbitMQ queue depth exceeds threshold. This reduces false positives and points to messaging bottlenecks.

Scrape pipeline
Exporters
Service and host exporters expose metrics endpoints.
Prometheus
Scrapes endpoints and stores data with labels for filtering.
Grafana
Builds dashboards and alerts backends.
Common Mistake
Using coarse scrape intervals that miss short-lived spikes in API latency.
Pro Tip
Label metrics by role so you can filter dashboards for controllers, compute nodes, or storage clusters quickly.

screens.title: Centralized Logging: ELK vs Splunk patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Centralized logging is essential for correlating events across OpenStack services and hosts. OpenStack services produce many log lines, and searching local files across controllers and compute nodes is slow and error-prone. Two common patterns are the ELK stack — Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana — and Splunk. Both centralize logs, index them for fast search, and enable dashboards and alerts. The main operational difference is deployment model and licensing; ELK is commonly self-hosted with open components, while Splunk is typically a commercial appliance. Regardless of the tool, centralization reduces the time to find the trace for an event. Concrete example: when a VM fails to boot, you can search across Nova A P I, scheduler, compute, and Neutron logs in one place to find the earliest error. A common mistake is shipping logs without consistent timestamps or missing context like request IDs; ensure your services include request identifiers and that log timestamps are synchronized via NTP. Key takeaway: central logging turns disparate local files into a cohesive event timeline you can query and alert on. Centralized Logging: ELK vs Splunk patterns means index logs centrally with request ids and synchronized timestamps to build a searchable event timeline across services.. In practical terms, why central logs matter and what each stack provides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Centralized Logging
Why centralize logs?

Central logs let you search across services, correlate errors, and build dashboards for trends and anomalies.

  • • Index logs for fast search across controllers and compute nodes.
  • • Retain logs long enough for post-mortem and compliance.
  • • Use request IDs to trace an event end-to-end.
Common Mistake

Sending logs without consistent timestamps or without request context makes correlation unreliable. Always enable NTP and include identifiers in logs.

Stack comparison
ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana)
Open components that index logs, transform them, and visualize results. Common in self-hosted environments.
Splunk
Commercial platform with integrated indexing, search, and alerting. Operational trade-offs include licensing and appliance models.
Concrete Example

When a VM fails to boot, search for the instance UUID across Nova API, scheduler, compute, and Neutron logs to find the earliest failing component.

screens.title: Using the OpenStack CLI and service logs
screens.narratorSegment: Effective troubleshooting begins with gathering verifiable evidence before making changes. The openstack CLI gives you high-level state: openstack service list shows registered services and their endpoints; openstack server show reveals instance state and fault information; openstack port show and openstack network agent list expose network status. Service logs supply timestamps, request IDs, and error traces. On RHEL hosts, journalctl -u. service -n 100 will show recent logs for a unit; use the follow option to watch live events during a restart. Also check system-level indicators like ip a for interface status and df -h for disk usage. A common misconception is trusting a single command; instead, collect a short set of outputs and correlate them with log traces and metrics. Concrete example: when a compute instance fails to boot, run openstack server show to capture the instance fault, then tail Nova A P I and Nova compute logs with journalctl to find the first failing stack frame. That evidence directs focused remediation rather than blind restarts. Using the OpenStack CLI and service logs means use cli commands and journalctl to gather a consistent set of outputs and correlate them with logs before acting.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Collect evidence first
keyIdea.text: Use CLI commands and journalctl to gather a consistent set of outputs and correlate them with logs before acting.

content.html:
Process Flow › CLI & Logs
Common Commands
# List OpenStack services
openstack service list

# Check Nova API logs (follow latest entries)
sudo journalctl -u openstack-nova-api.service -f

# Tail Neutron server logs
sudo journalctl -u openstack-neutron-server.service -f

# Show an instance
openstack server show
Note: replace <instance-id> with the affected instance UUID. Use systemctl status to check unit state if a service appears down.
Gathering evidence
  • • Capture openstack service list and relevant openstack server show output.
  • • Tail journalctl for implicated units and copy the first error lines.
  • • Check ip a and df -h for host network or disk issues.
Key Takeaway
Collect a minimal reproducible evidence set that includes CLI outputs and the relevant log excerpts before taking corrective actions.

screens.title: Simulated Nova API failure — terminal walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simulated Nova A P I failure with the exact commands you would run. Begin by listing OpenStack services to see if Nova A P I is registered and healthy. If a Compute service shows Error in Horizon, run openstack service list to confirm. Next, check the unit status: sudo systemctl status openstack-nova-api. service shows recent failures. Then tail the service logs using journalctl -u openstack-nova-api. service -n 50 -f to capture tracebacks and error messages. Remember to also check Nova Scheduler and Nova Compute logs because instance boot failures often span components. If logs show connection errors to RabbitMQ or the database, do not restart Nova first; verify that RabbitMQ and MariaDB are reachable and have no backlog. Use openstack network agent list to ensure Neutron agents are present if networking issues appear. A common misstep is restarting services without confirming dependencies; instead, collect logs, verify RabbitMQ and DB access, and only then perform targeted restarts. In practice, this sequence converts an initial Incident into reproducible troubleshooting steps and avoids introducing more variables. In practical terms, follow a realistic command sequence to locate the root cause. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Run service list, check unit status, tail service logs, and verify dependencies before changing state.

content.html:
Hands-on Demo › Nova API Failure
Terminal Sequence
# 1. List services
openstack service list

# 2. Check Nova API unit status
sudo systemctl status openstack-nova-api.service

# 3. Tail recent Nova API logs
sudo journalctl -u openstack-nova-api.service -n 50 -f

# 4. Check RabbitMQ backlog and agents
# (use appropriate rabbitmq or openstack agent commands)
openstack network agent list
Follow these steps to locate the first error line which often points to dependency problems such as RabbitMQ or database connectivity.
Concrete Example

When logs show "connection refused" to RabbitMQ, inspect RabbitMQ queues and connectivity before restarting Nova services; restarting Nova alone usually does not clear a messaging backlog.

Common Mistake

Restarting multiple services at once without isolating the root cause can obscure the original error and delay recovery.

screens.title: A disciplined troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A systematic troubleshooting approach prevents hasty decisions and speeds recovery. Start by defining the symptom and collecting evidence: record timestamps, affected services, and the exact error messages. Second, gather state: run openstack service list, openstack server show for affected instances, and openstack network agent list for networking checks. Third, collect logs using journalctl for the implicated units and central logging indices for correlated events across nodes. Fourth, check dependencies: ensure RabbitMQ, MariaDB, and Keystone are reachable and healthy. Fifth, form a hypothesis and test it in a narrow scope — for example, restart a single service or correct a configuration, then observe results. Always avoid broad restarts across many nodes. Misconception to avoid: assuming a single restart will fix all problems. Instead, make small changes with monitoring and log collection in place so you can roll back if needed. After resolution, document the root cause, remediation steps, and any action items such as improving alerts or scheduling maintenance. This workflow turns incidents into improvements. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow › Troubleshooting Workflow
Step-by-step
  1. Define the symptom and time window.
  2. Collect state via openstack CLI and system tools.
  3. Tail service logs and search central logs for correlated entries.
  4. Verify dependencies: RabbitMQ, DB, Keystone.
  5. Form a narrow hypothesis, test, and observe.
Example Scenario

If instances fail to boot and logs show messaging timeouts, verify RabbitMQ queue depth and connectivity. If backlog is present, address messaging or scaling rather than restarting compute nodes blindly.

Post-incident

Document root cause, remediation, and update runbooks and alerts to prevent recurrence.

screens.title: Network issues and Neutron agent checks
screens.narratorSegment: Networking problems often masquerade as compute failures. When a VM fails to boot or a service reports connectivity errors, check Neutron first. Use openstack network agent list to confirm agents are present and alive. On compute nodes, inspect Neutron agent logs for local failures. For host-level network issues, check ip a for interface state and ethtool or driver messages in journalctl. A common pitfall is assuming Nova is the only cause of boot failures while Neutron agents on compute nodes are down. Example: if openstack network agent list shows an agent in down state, tail the neutron agent logs on that compute node to find the cause; it may be an interface naming change, a firewall rule, or a service crash. Also verify that DHCP and metadata agents are functioning if instances cannot obtain network configuration. Key takeaway: validate that Neutron's agent layer is healthy before escalating to compute or A P I-level fixes, because networking failures often block instance creation even when Nova services are nominal. screens.title: Message queue and database dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: OpenStack services rely heavily on central dependencies: a message queue and a database. RabbitMQ mediates task and RPC traffic between services; when messages pile up or connections fail, services experience timeouts and delayed operations. MariaDB or PostgreSQL store the persistent state for services; corrupted or unavailable databases cause failures across the control plane. When troubleshooting, always verify RabbitMQ and the database after service errors. Check for backlog in RabbitMQ, node connectivity, and authentication errors. For databases, ensure your dump and restore scripts run and that database endpoints are reachable. Misconception: seeing a service error does not imply the service binary itself is the root cause; many service errors are symptoms of dependency failures. Concrete example: a large RabbitMQ backlog can cause Nova A P I to time out while posting tasks; investigate queue depth before restarting Nova services. Key takeaway: verify the health and performance of RabbitMQ and the database early in the investigation because these systems often explain widespread, cross-service errors. Why they matter

screens.title: Backup and recovery for control plane and data
screens.narratorSegment: Backups are non-negotiable. For a successful recovery you must protect three categories: databases, configuration files, and images. Databases (MariaDB or PostgreSQL) contain the canonical state for Keystone, Nova, Neutron, Cinder, and Glance. Use consistent dumps with mysqldump or pg_dump and verify integrity. Configuration files under /etc for each service hold integration details and must be preserved; without them restored services will have missing endpoints and broken authentication. Glance images and metadata must be backed up or replicated; if images are stored on Ceph, ensure Ceph pools are durable and you have an off-site strategy for critical images. Ceph's replication reduces data loss risk but does not replace a tested recovery plan. Always test your restore process. A common mistake is backing up only databases while neglecting configuration, which leaves you with data but not a runnable deployment. Concrete example: restore the database and /etc/nova/nova. conf files to a clean host, then re-register services to recover a minimal control plane. Key takeaway: backup both state and configuration, and rehearse restores so recovery time is predictable. content.html:
Definition › Backup & Recovery
Essential backups
  • • Databases: mysqldump or pg_dump for Keystone, Nova, Neutron, Cinder, Glance.
  • • Configuration files: /etc// directories for each service.
  • • Glance images and Ceph pool metadata: ensure durability or off-site copies.
Recovery considerations
A restore must produce a consistent control plane: import databases, restore configuration files, verify Keystone identity data, and re-register services if necessary. Testing recovery procedures regularly reduces surprises during real incidents.
Concrete Example
Restore MariaDB dumps, restore /etc/nova, then start nova-api and nova-scheduler in sequence while watching logs for migration errors.
Common Mistake
Backing up data but not configuration files leaves you unable to restore a working environment quickly.

screens.title: Upgrades and ongoing maintenance
screens.narratorSegment: Upgrades are complex and require planning. Use a test environment to run through the documented upgrade path and verify each step before touching production. For Red Hat OpenStack Platform, follow vendor upgrade guidance, perform package and certificate checks, and maintain consistent host patch levels. Routine maintenance tasks include rotating logs and cleaning up old snapshots and unused resources to avoid disk pressure, which can cause services to fail. Always build a rollback plan: snapshot or backup critical databases and configurations before an upgrade so you can return to a known state if a step fails. A common incorrect assumption is that Ceph replication alone eliminates the need for backups during upgrades; while Ceph provides data durability, control plane state and configuration still need independent recovery points. Concrete example: before a major platform upgrade, export database dumps, snapshot key config directories, and test service restarts in a staging cluster. Key takeaway: test upgrades, keep rollback paths, and automate maintenance checks where possible to reduce operational risk. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to operate and recover a production Red Hat OpenStack Platform cloud. We start by treating monitoring as the platform's sensory system: metrics and dashboards give you early warnings; centralized logs let you trace events across services; and a disciplined troubleshooting approach converts noisy alerts into root causes. You will see concrete examples with commands for identifying a Nova A P I failure, reading relevant service logs, and verifying dependent services like RabbitMQ and the database. We also cover backup components you must protect — databases, configuration files, and Glance images — and why Ceph's durability does not replace tested recovery procedures. Finally, you will learn upgrade and maintenance practices to reduce downtime and preserve a rollback path. As you follow the demonstrations, think about how your organization currently captures metrics, centralizes logs, and verifies recovery procedures. That question will guide the lab at the end: how would you adapt your backup strategy for OpenStack?

By the end of this chapter you will implement monitoring and logging, use CLI tools and service logs for targeted troubleshooting, design backup and recovery strategies for control plane and data, and apply best practices for upgrades and maintenance. Practically, implementing monitoring means configuring Prometheus to scrape exporters for Nova, Neutron, Cinder, and Keystone and creating Grafana dashboards that surface A P I latency and queue backlogs. Using CLI tools means you can run the openstack service list and inspect server, port, and agent status. For backups you will identify the databases to dump, the configuration directories to preserve, and how Glance images are stored. For upgrades you will plan test upgrades, maintain rollbacks, and keep certificates and host packages consistent. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone you can use as a checklist during audits and drills. These skills reduce mean time to resolution, help you validate change plans, and make recovery predictable.

This second objectives page maps each skill to verification actions and practical context. For monitoring, verify Prometheus scrapes target exporters and your Grafana dashboards show A P I latency and queue depth. For troubleshooting, practice with harmed services: use openstack service list, openstack server show, and journalctl to collect evidence before you change anything. For backups, build a recovery runbook that lists how to restore MariaDB or PostgreSQL dumps, recover /etc configuration files, and re-register Glance images if needed. For upgrades and maintenance, document the upgrade path, test it in a staging environment, and validate certificates and RHEL host packages after patching. Each card contains a short checklist you can use during drills. Practicing these actions and testing your fallback plan reduces time to full recovery and prevents silent gaps in your process.

Monitoring is more than checking whether services are up. For a Red Hat OpenStack Platform cloud you must monitor service health, performance metrics like C P U, R A M, disk input and output and network throughput, and A P I response times. These signals let you detect slowdowns before they become outages. A common mistake is only collecting host-level metrics and neglecting service-specific metrics, such as Nova scheduler queue depth or Neutron agent heartbeats. To be effective, configure exporters that expose service metrics to Prometheus and create Grafana panels for latency, error rates, and message queue depth. Use service-specific alerts that combine conditions — for example, high A P I latency together with a RabbitMQ backlog — to reduce false positives. Concrete example: if Grafana shows rising Nova A P I latency and Prometheus shows a growing RabbitMQ queue, suspect a messaging bottleneck rather than a compute node fault. Misconception: monitoring is not a replacement for logging; logs give the causal trace you need for root cause. Key takeaway: instrument services and hosts, tune alerts to reduce noise, and correlate metrics with logs to find the true issue.

Prometheus and Grafana form a compact monitoring architecture commonly used with Red Hat OpenStack Platform. Prometheus scrapes metrics from exporters exposed by OpenStack services or host exporters on RHEL. Those metrics are stored as time-series data and evaluated by alert rules. Grafana queries Prometheus to build dashboards that combine metrics across services. For example, a dashboard showing Nova A P I request latency, Nova scheduler backlog, and RabbitMQ queue depth gives a combined view that helps discriminate between compute, scheduling, and messaging problems. A common misstep is scraping only default exporters; ensure that service-specific exporters are enabled and that the scrape interval matches your alerting needs. Another practical tip: tag metrics with service and host labels so panels can filter by controller, compute, or storage nodes. Concrete example: set an alert for when Nova A P I p99 latency rises above a threshold while RabbitMQ queue length exceeds a limit; this pairing will point you to messaging saturation rather than transient compute slowness. Remember to archive long-term metrics if you need historical trend analysis during post-mortem investigations. Prometheus and Grafana for RHOSP means prometheus collects labeled metrics; grafana visualizes them. use combined panels and labels to find cause quickly.. In practical terms, how prometheus scrapes metrics and grafana surfaces service health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Centralized logging is essential for correlating events across OpenStack services and hosts. OpenStack services produce many log lines, and searching local files across controllers and compute nodes is slow and error-prone. Two common patterns are the ELK stack — Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana — and Splunk. Both centralize logs, index them for fast search, and enable dashboards and alerts. The main operational difference is deployment model and licensing; ELK is commonly self-hosted with open components, while Splunk is typically a commercial appliance. Regardless of the tool, centralization reduces the time to find the trace for an event. Concrete example: when a VM fails to boot, you can search across Nova A P I, scheduler, compute, and Neutron logs in one place to find the earliest error. A common mistake is shipping logs without consistent timestamps or missing context like request IDs; ensure your services include request identifiers and that log timestamps are synchronized via NTP. Key takeaway: central logging turns disparate local files into a cohesive event timeline you can query and alert on. Centralized Logging: ELK vs Splunk patterns means index logs centrally with request ids and synchronized timestamps to build a searchable event timeline across services.. Effective troubleshooting begins with gathering verifiable evidence before making changes. The openstack CLI gives you high-level state: openstack service list shows registered services and their endpoints; openstack server show reveals instance state and fault information; openstack port show and openstack network agent list expose network status. Service logs supply timestamps, request IDs, and error traces. On RHEL hosts, journalctl -u. service -n 100 will show recent logs for a unit; use the follow option to watch live events during a restart. Also check system-level indicators like ip a for interface status and df -h for disk usage. A common misconception is trusting a single command; instead, collect a short set of outputs and correlate them with log traces and metrics. Concrete example: when a compute instance fails to boot, run openstack server show to capture the instance fault, then tail Nova A P I and Nova compute logs with journalctl to find the first failing stack frame. That evidence directs focused remediation rather than blind restarts. Let's walk through a simulated Nova A P I failure with the exact commands you would run. Begin by listing OpenStack services to see if Nova A P I is registered and healthy. If a Compute service shows Error in Horizon, run openstack service list to confirm. Next, check the unit status: sudo systemctl status openstack-nova-api. service shows recent failures. Then tail the service logs using journalctl -u openstack-nova-api. service -n 50 -f to capture tracebacks and error messages. Remember to also check Nova Scheduler and Nova Compute logs because instance boot failures often span components. If logs show connection errors to RabbitMQ or the database, do not restart Nova first; verify that RabbitMQ and MariaDB are reachable and have no backlog. OpenStack services rely heavily on central dependencies: a message queue and a database. RabbitMQ mediates task and RPC traffic between services; when messages pile up or connections fail, services experience timeouts and delayed operations. MariaDB or PostgreSQL store the persistent state for services; corrupted or unavailable databases cause failures across the control plane. When troubleshooting, always verify RabbitMQ and the database after service errors. Check for backlog in RabbitMQ, node connectivity, and authentication errors. For databases, ensure your dump and restore scripts run and that database endpoints are reachable. Misconception: seeing a service error does not imply the service binary itself is the root cause; many service errors are symptoms of dependency failures. Backups are non-negotiable. For a successful recovery you must protect three categories: databases, configuration files, and images. Databases (MariaDB or PostgreSQL) contain the canonical state for Keystone, Nova, Neutron, Cinder, and Glance. Use consistent dumps with mysqldump or pg_dump and verify integrity. Configuration files under /etc for each service hold integration details and must be preserved; without them restored services will have missing endpoints and broken authentication. Glance images and metadata must be backed up or replicated; if images are stored on Ceph, ensure Ceph pools are durable and you have an off-site strategy for critical images. Ceph's replication reduces data loss risk but does not replace a tested recovery plan. Always test your restore process. A common mistake is backing up only databases while neglecting configuration, which leaves you with data but not a runnable deployment. Concrete example: restore the database and /etc/nova/nova. conf files to a clean host, then re-register services to recover a minimal control plane. Key takeaway: backup both state and configuration, and rehearse restores so recovery time is predictable. For Red Hat OpenStack Platform, follow vendor upgrade guidance, perform package and certificate checks, and maintain consistent host patch levels. Routine maintenance tasks include rotating logs and cleaning up old snapshots and unused resources to avoid disk pressure, which can cause services to fail. Always build a rollback plan: snapshot or backup critical databases and configurations before an upgrade so you can return to a known state if a step fails. These are the essential concepts to keep at hand. First, monitoring must include service-specific metrics, not just host metrics. Fourth, back up databases, configuration files, and images; verify restores. Fifth, test upgrades and maintain rollback plans.
